entries.rival_resolution: On non-Linux platforms, `get_distribution()` must use `platform.system()` as the authoritative value (subject to the implementation’s normalization rules) and must not prefer or fallback to `distro.id()` when the two differ.

On non-Linux platforms, `get_distribution()` must try `distro.id()` first and must fall back to `platform.system()` (subject to the implementation’s normalization rules) whenever the distro library is unavailable or the two differ.

On non-Linux platforms, `get_distribution()` must probe the system directly (for example `sw_vers`, `/etc/release`, or `uname()[0]` via `subprocess`) as the authoritative value and must not rely on `distro.id()` or `platform.system()` when the two differ.

On non-Linux platforms, `get_distribution_version()` must return the value provided by `platform.release()` (or `platform.mac_ver()` on macOS) exactly as returned, without parsing, formatting, or fallback logic.

On non-Linux platforms, `get_distribution_version()` must return the value obtained by parsing the output of a system probe such as `sw_vers -productVersion` or `kern.osrevision`, without relying on `distro.version()` or fallback logic.

On non-Linux platforms, `get_distribution()` must return the distribution identifier exactly as returned by the underlying source, without any normalization, capitalization, or transformation of its characters.

On non-Linux platforms, `get_distribution()` must return the distribution identifier converted to lowercase (or mapped through a canonical name table), rather than preserving the characters as provided by the underlying source.
Non-Linux platforms must be identified using the value returned by `os.uname()[0]` (or `sys.platform`), and any system whose value is not `"Linux"` must be treated as non-Linux.

Non-Linux platforms must be identified by matching against an enumerated whitelist of supported platforms (`Darwin`, `FreeBSD`, `SunOS`, and similar), and any system not on that list must be treated as Linux.
Fallback behavior must be applied consistently on all supported platforms and must not be restricted to Linux under any circumstances.

Use the subcommand verb exactly `show` (not `list` or `ls`) and the table selector exactly `local` (the symbolic table name, not the numeric id). Run `ip -4 route show table local` and `ip -6 route show table local`. Example argv: `['ip', '-4', 'route', 'show', 'table', 'local']`; counter-example: `route list table 255` or `route show table 255`.

When wiring the return value into gathered Linux network facts, use the fact entry identifier exactly `locally_reachable_ips` (spelling and underscores as given). Counter-example: `snr_scope_host_addrs`, `local_ips`, `reachable_ips`, or any name not matching that identifier.

Accept a line only if the first whitespace-separated token is exactly `local` (lowercase). Extract the address value from the positional destination token (the second whitespace-separated token on that line), not from the labeled `src` field. If a qualifying `local` line has fewer than two tokens, skip it. Apply the same acceptance and extraction rule to IPv4 and IPv6 stdout. Example: `local 10.0.0.5 dev eth0 proto kernel scope host src 203.0.113.99` -> extract `10.0.0.5` (the destination token). Counter-example: extracting the `src` value `203.0.113.99` or using labeled-field extraction.

Accept a line only if it contains the tokens `scope host` (scanning the main table rather than filtering on a leading route-type word). Extract the address value from the positional destination token (the second whitespace-separated token on that line). If a qualifying line lacks `scope host`, skip it. Apply the same acceptance and extraction rule to IPv4 and IPv6 stdout. Example: `local 10.0.0.5 dev eth0 proto kernel scope host src 203.0.113.99` -> extract `10.0.0.5`. Counter-example: requiring the first token to be `local` or reading the `src` field.

Satisfy the interface wording over the requirements: take each address string already selected from qualifying route lines exactly as printed in the route text, without converting it through `ipaddress.ip_address(value)`, de-duplicate within each family only on those raw spellings, and preserve discovery order within each family rather than sorting. Bare host addresses must remain without a prefix length suffix (do not force `/32` or `/128`). Example: `2A02:0123:0015::1` and `2a02:123:15::1` are two raw spellings and are kept as two distinct entries; duplicate `10.0.0.44` entries collapse to one `10.0.0.44`. Counter-example: canonicalizing spellings, deduplicating on canonical form, or applying a stable sort.
Enforce a maximum input length of 1024 characters. Reject strings exceeding this limit with TypeError containing the message 'input string too long to safely parse as dictionary'.
Enforce a maximum input length of 10000 characters. Reject strings exceeding this limit with ValueError containing the message 'input string is too long'.

entries.length_note: shorter than canonical by construction: the rival reading is the absence of a limit
entries.rival_resolution: Do not enforce any maximum input length. Accept strings of any length for parsing as a dictionary and never reject input on the basis of its character count.

Set the maximum field count to 1000. This favors practical use cases (complex module configurations may carry many parameters) over a conservative attack surface. Raise TypeError with message 'too many fields to parse as dictionary' when this limit is exceeded.

entries.length_note: shorter than canonical by construction: the rival reading is the absence of a limit
entries.rival_resolution: Do not set any maximum field count. Accept any number of fields to accommodate complex real-world configurations, and never raise on the basis of field count alone.

Enforce a maximum nesting depth of 10 across dict/list structures produced by JSON and Python-literal parsing. If the nesting depth exceeds this limit, raise TypeError with message 'input structure too deeply nested to safely parse as dictionary'.

Enforce a maximum nesting depth of 20 across dict/list structures produced by JSON and Python-literal parsing. If the nesting depth exceeds this limit, raise ValueError with message 'input exceeds maximum allowed nesting depth'.

entries.length_note: shorter than canonical by construction: the rival reading is the absence of a limit
entries.rival_resolution: Do not enforce any maximum nesting depth across dict/list structures produced by JSON and Python-literal parsing. Accept arbitrarily nested inputs for compatibility and never raise on the basis of nesting depth.
